variants.name: Coroutine Job cancellation and structured propagation
variants.implementation_notes: In Kotlin the token is the coroutine's Job from kotlinx.coroutines: cancel() requests cancellation, the request propagates to children through structured concurrency, and it materialises as CancellationException at the next suspension point. Code that does not suspend must cooperate explicitly with ensureActive() or isActive, or call yield() to both check cancellation and let other coroutines run; withTimeout derives a deadline child, and withContext(NonCancellable) or a finally block delimits the cleanup that must complete. The rule the documentation states - always rethrow CancellationException - is what keeps the tree consistent.
pitfalls: Catching CancellationException (or Exception/Throwable) without rethrowing swallows the request and leaves the coroutine running inside a cancelled scope, so the parent's join never returns.
Cancellation is cooperative: a tight CPU loop that neither suspends nor checks isActive is not cancelled - insert yield() or ensureActive() periodically.
Job.cancel() is asynchronous and returns immediately; use join() when the caller must know the coroutine has stopped, and remember that finally blocks, not the cancel call, do the cleanup.
Blocking JVM calls (Thread.sleep, BlockingQueue.take) ignore coroutine cancellation; wrap them in runInterruptible or move them to an interruptible API.

variants.name: Bridging to thread interruption with runInterruptible
variants.implementation_notes: Coroutine cancellation does not interrupt the underlying thread, so blocking code that only responds to interruption (Thread.sleep, blocking queues, interruptible I/O) needs a bridge: runInterruptible runs the block and converts the coroutine's cancellation into a thread interrupt, rethrowing the resulting InterruptedException as CancellationException once unwound. Use it at every boundary where Kotlin code calls an interruptible JVM API, and prefer dispatchers designed for blocking work (IO) so the interrupt does not land on a thread that must stay responsive. The rest of the pattern is unchanged - the Job remains the token; this variant only defines how the request reaches code that cannot observe it cooperatively.
pitfalls: Interruption can arrive between any two instructions of the block, so only interrupt-safe code belongs inside runInterruptible - blocking a mutex or a non-interruptible native call converts cancellation into a hang.

The interrupt status must be preserved: catching InterruptedException and not rethrowing (or clearing) it hides the cancellation and can leave the thread's flag in an unexpected state for the next task.

runInterruptible costs an extra dispatch; wrapping cheap non-blocking calls adds overhead without changing responsiveness, and Dispatchers.IO should be used so the interrupt targets a thread that may be blocked.
